Lecture 24

Lorentz groups and finite-dimensional representations

We build the double cover SL⁡(2,C)→SO⁡+(1,3)\SL(2,\C)\to\SO^+(1,3)SL(2,C)→SO+(1,3) from Hermitian 2×22\times22×2 matrices. We then classify the finite-dimensional irreducible continuous complex representations of both groups by complexifying the real Lie algebra.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Prove that SL⁡(2,C)→SO⁡+(1,3)\SL(2,\C)\to\SO^+(1,3)SL(2,C)→SO+(1,3) is a surjective covering homomorphism with kernel {±I}\{\pm I\}{±I}, and identify SL⁡(2,R)\SL(2,\R)SL(2,R) as the double cover of SO⁡+(1,2)\SO^+(1,2)SO+(1,2) inside it.
  • Identify sl(2,C)R⊗RC\sllie(2,\C)_\R\otimes_\R\Csl(2,C)R​⊗R​C with sl(2,C)⊕sl(2,C)\sllie(2,\C)\oplus\sllie(2,\C)sl(2,C)⊕sl(2,C).
  • Label the irreducible finite-dimensional continuous complex representations of SL⁡(2,C)\SL(2,\C)SL(2,C) by (jL,jR)(j_L,j_R)(jL​,jR​) and decide when they descend to SO⁡+(1,3)\SO^+(1,3)SO+(1,3).
  • Recognise Weyl spinors and four-vectors in this list.

In special relativity an event has coordinates x=(x0,x⃗)x=(x_0,\vec x)x=(x0​,x), with time x0x_0x0​ and position x⃗∈R3\vec x\in\R^3x∈R3. We use units in which light has speed 111. Inertial observers are related by linear maps that preserve the Minkowski form below. Relativistic fields take values in finite-dimensional representations of the Lorentz group or its double cover SL⁡(2,C)\SL(2,\C)SL(2,C).

24.1 Minkowski space and the Lorentz group

Let e0,…,e3e_0,\dots,e_3e0​,…,e3​ be the standard basis of R4\R^4R4. The Minkowski form is ⟨x,y⟩=x0y0−x⃗⋅y⃗=xTηy,η=diag⁡(1,−1,−1,−1).\langle x,y\rangle=x_0y_0-\vec x\cdot\vec y=x^T\eta y,\qquad \eta=\diag(1,-1,-1,-1).⟨x,y⟩=x0​y0​−x⋅y​=xTηy,η=diag(1,−1,−1,−1).

Since ⟨Λe0,Λe0⟩=1\langle\Lambda e_0,\Lambda e_0\rangle=1⟨Λe0​,Λe0​⟩=1, Λ002=1+Λ102+Λ202+Λ302≥1.\Lambda_{00}^2=1+\Lambda_{10}^2+\Lambda_{20}^2+\Lambda_{30}^2\ge1 .Λ002​=1+Λ102​+Λ202​+Λ302​≥1. Definition 24.3. The proper orthochronous Lorentz group is SO⁡+(1,3)={Λ∈O⁡(1,3):det⁡Λ=1, Λ00≥1}.\SO^+(1,3)=\{\Lambda\in\operatorname{O}(1,3):\det\Lambda=1,\ \Lambda_{00}\ge1\}.SO+(1,3)={Λ∈O(1,3):detΛ=1, Λ00​≥1}.

By Steps 2 and 4, SO⁡+(1,3)=φ(SL⁡(2,C))\SO^+(1,3)=\varphi(\SL(2,\C))SO+(1,3)=φ(SL(2,C)) is connected. A continuous surjective homomorphism of connected Lie groups with bijective differential is a covering map (Lecture 4). Its fibres are cosets of ker⁡φ={±I}\ker\varphi=\{\pm I\}kerφ={±I}, so it has two sheets. 

Formula (24.2) gives dφ(Xk)=Jkd\varphi(X_k)=J_kdφ(Xk​)=Jk​ and dφ(iXk)=Kkd\varphi(iX_k)=K_kdφ(iXk​)=Kk​ for every kkk. The case k=3k=3k=3 is the diagonal computation of Example 24.4, Exercise 24.1 treats k=1k=1k=1, and the case k=2k=2k=2 is identical. The brackets [Xi,Xj]=ϵijkXk[X_i,X_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}X_k[Xi​,Xj​]=ϵijk​Xk​ then transfer through dφd\varphidφ: [Ji,Jj]=ϵijkJk,[Ji,Kj]=ϵijkKk,[Ki,Kj]=−ϵijkJk.[J_i,J_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}J_k,\qquad[J_i,K_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}K_k,\qquad[K_i,K_j]=-\epsilon_{ijk}J_k .[Ji​,Jj​]=ϵijk​Jk​,[Ji​,Kj​]=ϵijk​Kk​,[Ki​,Kj​]=−ϵijk​Jk​.

Steps 2 and 4 of the proof are the Cartan decomposition of Lecture 20, for the real algebra sl(2,C)R\sllie(2,\C)_\Rsl(2,C)R​ with k=su(2)\algk=\suu(2)k=su(2) and p=i su(2)\algp=i\,\suu(2)p=isu(2). Step 2 writes A=UPA=UPA=UP, with U∈SU⁡(2)U\in\SU(2)U∈SU(2) and P=exp⁡Y2P=\exp Y_2P=expY2​ for a traceless Hermitian Y2Y_2Y2​. So φ(A)=φ(U)φ(P)\varphi(A)=\varphi(U)\varphi(P)φ(A)=φ(U)φ(P), which is a boost followed by a rotation. Step 4 writes the same kind of element in the other order, as a rotation followed by a boost.

The same construction one dimension down

The construction also works for the real subgroup SL⁡(2,R)\SL(2,\R)SL(2,R) of SL⁡(2,C)\SL(2,\C)SL(2,C). It then relates SL⁡(2,R)\SL(2,\R)SL(2,R) to a Lorentz group with two space coordinates. Let R1,2\R^{1,2}R1,2 be the subspace {x∈R4:x2=0}\{x\in\R^4:x_2=0\}{x∈R4:x2​=0}, with the form x02−x12−x32x_0^2-x_1^2-x_3^2x02​−x12​−x32​. Proposition 24.6. Each φ(A)\varphi(A)φ(A) with A∈SL⁡(2,R)A\in\SL(2,\R)A∈SL(2,R) fixes e2e_2e2​ and preserves R1,2\R^{1,2}R1,2. Restriction to R1,2\R^{1,2}R1,2 gives a surjective homomorphism SL⁡(2,R)→SO⁡+(1,2)\SL(2,\R)\to\SO^+(1,2)SL(2,R)→SO+(1,2) with kernel {±I}\{\pm I\}{±I}.

So Lecture 21, Lecture 22 and Lecture 23 studied the double cover of the Lorentz group of two space coordinates and one time. This is why Bargmann’s paper, cited in Lecture 23, has the title Irreducible unitary representations of the Lorentz group.

24.3 Complexifying the Lorentz algebra

This section rests on one change of basis. In the complexified Lorentz algebra so(1,3)⊗RC\soo(1,3)\otimes_\R\Cso(1,3)⊗R​C, the elements 12(Jk−iKk)\frac12(J_k-iK_k)21​(Jk​−iKk​) obey the brackets of su(2)\suu(2)su(2). So do the elements 12(Jk+iKk)\frac12(J_k+iK_k)21​(Jk​+iKk​), and the two sets commute. We now derive this.

By the double-cover theorem, Theorem 24.5, so(1,3)≅sl(2,C)R\soo(1,3)\cong\sllie(2,\C)_\Rso(1,3)≅sl(2,C)R​. A complex representation of this real algebra need not be complex linear. For example, Y↦YˉY\mapsto\bar YY↦Yˉ is a real Lie algebra automorphism that is not complex linear. Complexification treats both kinds together.

Let g\gg be a real Lie algebra and VVV a finite-dimensional complex space. A real Lie algebra map ρ:g→gl(V)\rho:\g\to\gl(V)ρ:g→gl(V) extends uniquely to a complex-linear Lie algebra map ρC(Y⊗z)=zρ(Y)\rho_\C(Y\otimes z)=z\rho(Y)ρC​(Y⊗z)=zρ(Y) on g⊗RC\g\otimes_\R\Cg⊗R​C. A complex subspace is ρ\rhoρ-invariant if and only if it is ρC\rho_\CρC​-invariant. A linear map intertwines two such maps ρ\rhoρ if and only if it intertwines their extensions.

The real algebra sl(2,C)R\sllie(2,\C)_\Rsl(2,C)R​ carries its own operator MMM, given by M(Y)=iYM(Y)=iYM(Y)=iY. It satisfies M2=−1M^2=-1M2=−1 and [MY,Z]=M[Y,Z][MY,Z]=M[Y,Z][MY,Z]=M[Y,Z]. After complexifying, M⊗1M\otimes1M⊗1 has the eigenvalues iii and −i-i−i. Its eigenspaces are ideals, since [(M⊗1)u,v]=(M⊗1)[u,v][(M\otimes1)u,v]=(M\otimes1)[u,v][(M⊗1)u,v]=(M⊗1)[u,v]. They commute: if uuu and vvv have eigenvalues iii and −i-i−i, then i[u,v]=(M⊗1)[u,v]=−i[u,v]i[u,v]=(M\otimes1)[u,v]=-i[u,v]i[u,v]=(M⊗1)[u,v]=−i[u,v]. The next proposition identifies these ideals with two copies of sl(2,C)\sllie(2,\C)sl(2,C). Under it, M⊗1M\otimes1M⊗1 becomes multiplication by iii on the first copy and by −i-i−i on the second.

Proposition 24.7. The complex-linear map ι:sl(2,C)R⊗RC→sl(2,C)⊕sl(2,C),Y⊗z↦(zY, zYˉ),\iota:\sllie(2,\C)_\R\otimes_\R\C\to\sllie(2,\C)\oplus\sllie(2,\C),\qquad Y\otimes z\mapsto(zY,\,z\bar Y),ι:sl(2,C)R​⊗R​C→sl(2,C)⊕sl(2,C),Y⊗z↦(zY,zYˉ), is an isomorphism of complex Lie algebras.

Proof. The pair (zY,zYˉ)(zY,z\bar Y)(zY,zYˉ) is real bilinear in (Y,z)(Y,z)(Y,z), so ι\iotaι is well defined and complex linear. Complex conjugation of matrices preserves brackets, so ι([Y⊗z,Y′⊗z′])=(zz′[Y,Y′], zz′[Yˉ,Yˉ′])=[ι(Y⊗z),ι(Y′⊗z′)].\iota([Y\otimes z,Y'\otimes z'])=\bigl(zz'[Y,Y'],\,zz'[\bar Y,\bar Y']\bigr)=[\iota(Y\otimes z),\iota(Y'\otimes z')] .ι([Y⊗z,Y′⊗z′])=(zz′[Y,Y′],zz′[Yˉ,Yˉ′])=[ι(Y⊗z),ι(Y′⊗z′)]. A general element Y⊗1+Y′⊗iY\otimes1+Y'\otimes iY⊗1+Y′⊗i has image (Y+iY′, Yˉ+iYˉ′)(Y+iY',\,\bar Y+i\bar Y')(Y+iY′,Yˉ+iYˉ′). Hence Yˉ′=0\bar Y'=0Yˉ′=0, so Y′=0Y'=0Y′=0 and Y=0Y=0Y=0. 

Since iXk‾=−iXˉk\overline{iX_k}=-i\bar X_kiXk​​=−iXˉk​, we have ι(Xk⊗1)=(Xk,Xˉk)\iota(X_k\otimes1)=(X_k,\bar X_k)ι(Xk​⊗1)=(Xk​,Xˉk​) and ι(iXk⊗i)=(−Xk,Xˉk)\iota(iX_k\otimes i)=(-X_k,\bar X_k)ι(iXk​⊗i)=(−Xk​,Xˉk​). Hence the elements XkL=12(Xk⊗1−iXk⊗i),XkR=12(Xk⊗1+iXk⊗i)X^L_k=\tfrac12(X_k\otimes1-iX_k\otimes i),\qquad X^R_k=\tfrac12(X_k\otimes1+iX_k\otimes i)XkL​=21​(Xk​⊗1−iXk​⊗i),XkR​=21​(Xk​⊗1+iXk​⊗i) satisfy ι(XkL)=(Xk,0)\iota(X^L_k)=(X_k,0)ι(XkL​)=(Xk​,0) and ι(XkR)=(0,Xˉk)\iota(X^R_k)=(0,\bar X_k)ι(XkR​)=(0,Xˉk​). Every finite-dimensional continuous complex representation of SL⁡(2,C)\SL(2,\C)SL(2,C) is a direct sum of representations (jL,jR)(j_L,j_R)(jL​,jR​). This follows from Weyl’s complete reducibility theorem for the semisimple algebra sl(2,C)⊕sl(2,C)\sllie(2,\C)\oplus\sllie(2,\C)sl(2,C)⊕sl(2,C), transferred as in the proof.

The representations (j,0)(j,0)(j,0) are the holomorphic extensions from SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2) given by Lecture 14, since the entries of S2j(A)S^{2j}(A)S2j(A) are polynomials in the entries of AAA.

Only (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) admits an invariant inner product. The reason is that a boost generator has the nonzero real eigenvalue jL+jRj_L+j_RjL​+jR​ on every (jL,jR)≠(0,0)(j_L,j_R)\ne(0,0)(jL​,jR​)=(0,0). Exercise 24.6 gives the proof. So every nontrivial continuous unitary representation of this group is infinite-dimensional. Such representations exist. They are induced from the upper triangular subgroup, as in Lecture 22, and their models use the sphere of light rays. We do not study them; see Knapp, Representation Theory of Semisimple Groups, Chapter II, Section 4.

In physics, let a field ψ\psiψ take values in a representation space VVV with matrices D(A)D(A)D(A). Its transformation is ψ′(x)=D(A)ψ(φ(A)−1x).\psi'(x)=D(A)\psi(\varphi(A)^{-1}x).ψ′(x)=D(A)ψ(φ(A)−1x). The label (jL,jR)(j_L,j_R)(jL​,jR​) classifies the components of ψ\psiψ. It does not describe the unitary Hilbert space of particle states, which is the subject of Lecture 25.

24.5 Weyl spinors and four-vectors

Example 24.10 (Weyl spinors). The representation (12,0)(\frac12,0)(21​,0) is C2\C^2C2 with A↦AA\mapsto AA↦A. The representation (0,12)(0,\frac12)(0,21​) is C2\C^2C2 with A↦AˉA\mapsto\bar AA↦Aˉ. Physicists call their vectors left-handed and right-handed Weyl spinors. The choice of hands is a convention. By the classification theorem, Theorem 24.9, the two representations are inequivalent. A direct check uses traces. For A=diag⁡(2i,−i2)∈SL⁡(2,C)A=\diag(2i,-\frac i2)\in\SL(2,\C)A=diag(2i,−2i​)∈SL(2,C), tr⁡A=3i2,tr⁡Aˉ=−3i2.\tr A=\tfrac{3i}2,\qquad\tr\bar A=-\tfrac{3i}2 .trA=23i​,trAˉ=−23i​. Equivalent representations have equal traces. These traces differ, so the trace check confirms that the two representations are inequivalent. Both representations restrict to V1V_1V1​ on SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2). Both send −I-I−I to −1-1−1, so neither descends to SO⁡+(1,3)\SO^+(1,3)SO+(1,3). The Dirac representation (12,0)⊕(0,12)(\frac12,0)\oplus(0,\frac12)(21​,0)⊕(0,21​) also sends −I-I−I to −1-1−1, so it does not descend either.

Example 24.11 (Four-vectors). Let Ψ:C2⊗C2→M2(C)\Psi:\C^2\otimes\C^2\to M_2(\C)Ψ:C2⊗C2→M2​(C) be the linear isomorphism given by Ψ(ξ⊗ζ)=ξζT\Psi(\xi\otimes\zeta)=\xi\zeta^TΨ(ξ⊗ζ)=ξζT. The map Ψ\PsiΨ sends ei⊗eje_i\otimes e_jei​⊗ej​ to the matrix unit EijE_{ij}Eij​. For A∈SL⁡(2,C)A\in\SL(2,\C)A∈SL(2,C), Ψ(Aξ⊗Aˉζ)=Aξ(Aˉζ)T=AξζTAˉT=A Ψ(ξ⊗ζ) A∗.\Psi(A\xi\otimes\bar A\zeta)=A\xi(\bar A\zeta)^T=A\xi\zeta^T\bar A^T=A\,\Psi(\xi\otimes\zeta)\,A^* .Ψ(Aξ⊗Aˉζ)=Aξ(Aˉζ)T=AξζTAˉT=AΨ(ξ⊗ζ)A∗. So D(12,12)(A)D^{(\frac12,\frac12)}(A)D(21​,21​)(A) becomes Z↦AZA∗Z\mapsto AZA^*Z↦AZA∗ on M2(C)=H⊕iHM_2(\C)=\mathcal H\oplus i\mathcal HM2​(C)=H⊕iH. This action preserves H\mathcal HH and acts there by φ(A)\varphi(A)φ(A). Hence (12,12)(\frac12,\frac12)(21​,21​) is equivalent to C4=R4⊗RC\C^4=\R^4\otimes_\R\CC4=R4⊗R​C with φ(A)\varphi(A)φ(A) extended complex-linearly. Since 2⋅12+2⋅12=22\cdot\frac12+2\cdot\frac12=22⋅21​+2⋅21​=2 is even, the representation (12,12)(\frac12,\frac12)(21​,21​) descends by the descent criterion of Theorem 24.9. The descended representation is the defining representation of SO⁡+(1,3)\SO^+(1,3)SO+(1,3) on C4\C^4C4.

Two checks are consistent with this identification. First, the restriction rule of Theorem 24.9(c) predicts V0⊕V2V_0\oplus V_2V0​⊕V2​ on SU⁡(2)\SU(2)SU(2). Indeed U∈SU⁡(2)U\in\SU(2)U∈SU(2) acts by Z↦UZU−1Z\mapsto UZU^{-1}Z↦UZU−1. It fixes III, which spans the time direction. 24.7 Summary

The action X↦AXA∗X\mapsto AXA^*X↦AXA∗ on Hermitian matrices preserves det⁡X=⟨x,x⟩\det X=\langle x,x\rangledetX=⟨x,x⟩. It gives a two-sheeted covering φ:SL⁡(2,C)→SO⁡+(1,3)\varphi:\SL(2,\C)\to\SO^+(1,3)φ:SL(2,C)→SO+(1,3) with kernel {±I}\{\pm I\}{±I}. Its restriction to real matrices is the double cover SL⁡(2,R)→SO⁡+(1,2)\SL(2,\R)\to\SO^+(1,2)SL(2,R)→SO+(1,2). The map ι\iotaι identifies the complexified Lorentz algebra with sl(2,C)⊕sl(2,C)\sllie(2,\C)\oplus\sllie(2,\C)sl(2,C)⊕sl(2,C). Up to equivalence, the irreducible finite-dimensional continuous representations of SL⁡(2,C)\SL(2,\C)SL(2,C) are the (jL,jR)(j_L,j_R)(jL​,jR​), given by S2jL(A)⊗S2jR(Aˉ)S^{2j_L}(A)\otimes S^{2j_R}(\bar A)S2jL​(A)⊗S2jR​(Aˉ). Exactly those with 2jL+2jR2j_L+2j_R2jL​+2jR​ even descend to SO⁡+(1,3)\SO^+(1,3)SO+(1,3). Weyl spinors are (12,0)(\frac12,0)(21​,0) and (0,12)(0,\frac12)(0,21​), and four-vectors are (12,12)(\frac12,\frac12)(21​,21​).
